name: Bulk and cut / body recomposition

lead: Bulking means eating in a surplus to gain muscle, cutting means eating in a deficit to lose fat while keeping muscle, and recomposition tries to do both at once. The cycle comes from bodybuilding, where competitors build through an off-season and begin cutting about 12-14 weeks before a contest.

A surplus supplies energy for muscle growth with resistance training, and a deficit strips fat to reveal the muscle. In looksmaxxing communities some advocate bulking to add size, others recomposition to avoid fat gain. The sources reviewed contain no controlled trials of the strategies themselves.

paras: Users alternate bulk and cut phases of varying lengths with lifting throughout, or hold calories near maintenance with high protein for slow recomposition. Some forum members also discuss drug adjuncts.
Some fat gain is expected in bulks, and a large deficit raises the risk of muscle loss. Muscle retention during cuts is described as uncertain.

angle.text: A calorie surplus with training builds muscle and a deficit phase strips fat, leaving a more muscular, leaner look. The approach comes from bodybuilding, and the sources reviewed contain no controlled trials of it.

lead: Bulk and cut cycling and body recomposition are ways of organizing eating and training to build a more muscular, leaner physique. A bulk is a period of eating in a calorie surplus to support muscle growth, a cut is a period of eating in a deficit to lose fat and reveal the muscle underneath, and recomposition (recomp) aims to gain muscle and lose fat at the same time.[1]

People use these approaches to change shape rather than simply weight: more shoulder, chest and arm size, a more defined waist and a lower body-fat look. The bulk-and-cut cycle comes from bodybuilding, where competitors traditionally gain muscle through most of the year in an off-season and then cut fat for roughly 12 to 14 weeks before a contest, according to Wikipedia. Wikipedia also says protein and food supplements for bulking up and cutting down became popular in the 1950s and 1960s alongside bodybuilding magazines.

A 2026 narrative review in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition reports that controlled trials show recomposition can occur when progressive resistance training, adequate protein and an appropriate energy prescription are combined, with effects largest in untrained people and those with more body fat.[1] Looksmaxxing forums discuss which approach suits skinny-fat, lean and overweight starting points, and how long bulks and cuts should last.[2][3][4]
infobox: More muscle with lower body fat
Clean bulk, dirty bulk, skinny fat, flexible dieting

paras: Wikipedia says bulking and cutting is considered effective because of the established link between muscle growth and a positive energy balance, while noting that it is unclear whether enough muscle is kept during the cut for the process to pay off. It adds that a larger surplus or longer bulk adds more fat, and that a bigger cutting deficit speeds weight loss but raises the risk of losing muscle.

Wikipedia distinguishes clean bulking, which aims to add muscle with little fat, takes longer and depends on hitting calorie targets, often with moderate carbohydrate and protein and low fat, from dirty bulking, an unmonitored large surplus that gives faster gains in size and strength but more fat and usually calls for a more aggressive cut afterwards. Some lifters find dirty bulking psychologically easier because it removes strict meal planning.

Recomposition is defined in the research literature as a concurrent increase in fat-free or skeletal muscle mass and decrease in fat mass within the same period.[1] It is usually pursued with training near maintenance calories or a modest deficit and high protein, rather than the alternating swings of a bulk-and-cut cycle.[1][5]

Wikipedia places the popularity of bulking and cutting diets and supplements in the 1950s and 1960s, alongside bodybuilding magazines; it does not give a precise date for the cycle's origin. In competitive bodybuilding the structure is a long off-season of surplus eating and heavy training, followed by a pre-contest diet; final-stage preparation combines carbohydrate loading and dehydration to maximise definition and vascularity, and most competitors also tan and shave before competing.

A 2014 review by Helms, Aragon and Fitschen in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition set out evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation. It suggested diets producing bodyweight loss of about 0.5 to 1% per week, protein of 2.3 to 3.1 g/kg of lean mass per day and 15 to 30% of calories from fat, reported that meal timing and frequency had little effect on fat loss or lean mass retention, and described dehydration practices before competition as potentially dangerous.[6] This paper is often cited in lifting communities as a reference for cutting.

More recent research has shifted attention to recomposition outside competition. A 2022 study in older women, a 2024 Frontiers in Nutrition editorial and a 2026 narrative review each address how muscle gain and fat loss can occur together.[1][7][8]

Common variants in lifting communities include long bulks followed by short cuts, a minibulk or lean bulk with a small surplus, alternating higher and lower calorie days, and recomposition at or near maintenance calories. Skinny-fat individuals, meaning people with low muscle mass and relatively high body fat at a normal weight, are the group most often discussed as starting with recomposition.[2][3]

A 2021 randomised trial in resistance-trained individuals compared flexible and rigid dieting approaches in people seeking to optimise their physiques, an angle also discussed in bodybuilding circles as flexible dieting.[9]

On looksmax.org, threads cover recomposition for skinny-fat people, with one opening that recomposition is about maximizing muscle and minimizing body fat.[2] Another thread argues that skinny-fat and overweight people should do something other than recomp.[3] A further thread discusses how to recomp down with minimal muscle loss in natural lifters.[4] In one thread a poster planned alternating three-month bulks and one-month cuts to avoid getting "fluffy", and replies disagreed about combining an appetite-suppressing drug with bulking.[10]
On T Nation, members ask how to set calorie targets for recomp, what to expect after a layoff, and whether recomp remains possible after two years of training.[11][12][13]

Researchers have examined how fast a cut should be and how much protein helps hold on to muscle during one. In a 2011 randomised trial of 24 elite athletes by Garthe and colleagues, both a slow weight-loss group (target 0.7% of bodyweight per week) and a fast group (1.4% per week) lost about 5.5% of bodyweight over the study while doing four resistance sessions a week; lean mass rose about 2.1% in the slow group and was unchanged in the fast group.[14] The authors concluded that athletes wanting to gain lean mass during weight loss should aim for the slower rate.[14]

A 2016 single-blind trial by Longland and colleagues randomised 40 young men to a roughly 40% energy deficit plus resistance and interval training six days a week for four weeks. The group eating 2.4 g/kg per day of protein gained about 1.2 kg of lean mass and lost 4.8 kg of fat, while the group eating 1.2 g/kg gained 0.1 kg and lost 3.5 kg.[15]

Reviews of eating disorder and body-image research in competitive bodybuilders report that dietary rigidity, orthorexia risk and post-competition binge eating occur in some competitors, though direct data are limited and the studies are cross-sectional.[16][17]

Wikipedia reports that aggressive cutting can be physically and mentally taxing and that dirty bulking can harm cardiovascular health and insulin sensitivity over time; it cites intentional dehydration and extreme weight changes as risk factors in studies linking bodybuilding to higher mortality, including sudden cardiac death. Forum discussions of drug adjuncts alongside bulking, such as appetite suppressants or fat-loss drugs, have not been studied for this purpose.[10]

A 2026 review of randomized trials and meta-analyses reports that resistance training with higher protein, typically about 1.6 to 2.4 g/kg per day, is the most consistent strategy for recomposition, with larger effects in untrained and higher-adiposity people and smaller effects in trained or lean athletes.[1]

A 2026 randomized trial of resistance-trained participants compared isocaloric and moderate-deficit high-protein diets with a control over 10 weeks of training; the deficit group reduced fat mass by 2.94 kg.[18]

A 2022 analysis of 130 untrained older women across six studies explored protein intake and recomposition after 24 weeks of resistance training and reported that moderate and higher protein intakes promoted superior recomposition.[7] A 2023 study in older women with different fat mass levels also examined recomposition and phase angle after resistance training.[5] A 2024 Frontiers in Nutrition editorial surveys new work on the topic.[8]

lore.intro: Recomp versus bulk-and-cut is a recurring debate on looksmax.org and T Nation, especially for skinny-fat beginners and long-time lifters.[2][3][13]
